title: Why are genealogies Included?
summary: Biblical genealogies do different kinds of work. Some trace descent, some link one story to another, some organize peoples or returning families, and Matthew and Luke use genealogies to place Jesus within Israel’s story. The surrounding passage shows which purpose matters in each case.
historical_context: The cited texts show genealogies and family lists being used within particular biblical settings: Genesis traces generations and peoples, Ruth closes with a line leading to David, Ezra lists families returning from exile, and Matthew and Luke place Jesus within genealogical lines. These examples show what the passages do; this entry has no separate source for broad claims about how ancient societies generally used genealogies.
canonical_context: Genesis 5 repeats a pattern of descendants, ages, and death; Genesis 10 organizes peoples by their lines; and Genesis 11 traces a line from Shem to Abram. Ruth 4 ends with a genealogy from Perez to David, linking the family story to Israel’s future king. Ezra 2 lists families among those returning from exile. Matthew 1 opens its Gospel by locating Jesus in relation to Abraham and David and arranging the names in three groups; Luke 3 traces Jesus’ line backward to Adam. These lists share a family-line form, but their placement and purpose differ.
literary_context: Notice where each genealogy appears. Genesis 5 and 11 use family lines to carry the story forward; Genesis 10 pauses to map peoples; Ruth places David’s line at the close of a family narrative; Ezra 2 uses lists within a return account; Matthew opens with Jesus’ genealogy; and Luke places one after Jesus’ baptism and before his public ministry. The literary position helps explain what the list contributes.
covenantal_significance: Some genealogies connect family lines with promises and leadership: Genesis moves from Abram’s ancestors into the promise story, Ruth 4 links a family account to David, and Matthew 1 places Jesus in relation to Abraham and David. Others serve different purposes, such as Genesis 10’s account of peoples or Ezra 2’s list of returning families. Genealogy is not automatically a messianic prediction; the text’s setting determines its significance.
canonical_role: Why are genealogies Included? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

related_objects.notes: Luke traces the line back to Adam

interpretive_notes.note: A genealogy can carry historical claims while also serving a literary or theological purpose. Read the names alongside the surrounding text: Genesis 5 marks a repeated mortality pattern, Ruth 4 links a family story to David, and Matthew 1 frames the Gospel’s account of Jesus. Do not assume every list serves the same purpose.

Genealogies can show continuity, but the specific continuity varies. Ruth 4 leads to David; Ezra 2 identifies families in the return list; Matthew 1 connects Jesus with Abraham and David. Only describe a promise or messianic connection where the passage itself or a later biblical text makes that link.
